phase1.explanation:
Remember how I said I build with blueprints? [[key:An abstract class is an incomplete blueprint on purpose]] — and that's actually the whole point of it.

Look at Shape in the code below. It knows every shape has a color, and it knows every shape needs a displayColor() method — so it writes that part for you. But it deliberately leaves area() and perimeter() blank. Why? Because Shape itself doesn't know how to calculate the area of "a shape in general." A circle's area formula and a rectangle's area formula have nothing in common — only Circle and Rectangle actually know how to fill that blank in for themselves.

That's what the [[term:abstract]] keyword means on a method: [[warn:no body, just a promise]]. abstract double area(); is Shape saying "every one of my subclasses WILL have an area() method — I just can't write it myself."

And because Shape is incomplete on purpose, Java won't let you build one directly. [[warn:new Shape("Red") is a compile error]] — you can't build from a blueprint that's missing pieces. You can only build a Circle or a Rectangle, because those blueprints are actually finished.

Here's the part I think is genuinely neat: once Circle and Rectangle each fill in area() and perimeter() their own way, you can treat them both as "just a Shape" in the rest of your code — look at the loop at the bottom of main(), it doesn't care whether each item is a Circle or a Rectangle, it just calls area() and trusts each one to know how to answer. That's [[term:polymorphism]] in action, and abstract classes are what make it possible to write it this cleanly.

Quick recap of what an abstract class can and can't do:
It CAN have fields, constructors, and fully-written (concrete) methods, same as any class — displayColor() up there is a perfectly normal method. It CAN have abstract methods with no body, which is the part that's new. What it CAN'T do is be instantiated directly with new — ever.

And [[key:every non-abstract subclass MUST implement every abstract method it inherits]] — Java will refuse to compile otherwise. No skipping the parts of the blueprint you don't feel like finishing.
phase1.openingDialogue: Time to build something on purpose incomplete~ Trust me, it'll make sense.

phase2.errorMessage:
Circle.java:10: error: Circle is not abstract and does not override abstract method area() in Shape
class Circle extends Shape {
^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
Circle extends Shape, but never actually writes an area() method of its own. [[warn:Every non-abstract subclass has to implement every abstract method it inherits]] — no exceptions, no "I'll get to it later."

Java's compiler is actually pretty clear about this one, if you read the error closely: it's telling you Circle isn't abstract itself, so it's not allowed to leave area() unfinished.

You've basically got two honest options here: actually write the area() method inside Circle — which is what you want 99% of the time — or mark Circle abstract too, which just pushes the problem one level down (and means you still can't build a Circle directly, which usually isn't what you wanted).

[[key:The compiler is doing you a favor here]], honestly — it's making sure nobody accidentally ships a shape that doesn't know how to calculate its own area.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a subclass gets lazy about its promises~

mcq.question:
Which of these can you do with an abstract class?

A) Create an object directly with new Shape()
B) Leave an abstract method with no body, as long as every non-abstract subclass implements it
C) Skip implementing an abstract method in a subclass if you're in a hurry
D) Have zero concrete methods — abstract classes can only have abstract ones

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create an abstract class Appliance with:
• Field: brand (String)
• Constructor
• Concrete method: turnOn() — prints "[brand] is turning on"
• Abstract method: operate()

Create WashingMachine and Microwave subclasses:
• Each implements operate() with their own behavior
• WashingMachine: prints "[brand] is washing clothes"
• Microwave: prints "[brand] is heating food"

In main, create an array of Appliance and call both methods on each.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: abstract classes and interfaces solve a similar problem, but Java actually let classes implement multiple interfaces long before it allowed extending multiple classes — that's precisely why interfaces exist as a separate concept at all. An abstract class is a blueprint you can only build ONE of underneath your class; an interface is more like a contract you can sign as many of as you want. We'll get to interfaces properly soon, and this abstract-class instinct will make them click faster.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~

hoverNotes.Circle: The concrete (fully finished) subclass in this example — it fills in every abstract method Shape leaves blank.
hoverNotes.Rectangle: Another concrete subclass of Shape — same blueprint, different shape-specific math.
